title: Wines That Don't Give You a Headache: What to Buy and Avoid
excerpt: Which wines are least likely to give you a headache? The real triggers (alcohol, histamine, tannins, sulfites), a shopping list by trigger, and the wines to skip.
metaDescription: Which wines are least likely to cause a headache? Low-alcohol picks, red vs white, sulfites, histamine, clean wine claims, and which bottles to avoid.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** no wine is guaranteed headache-free, because the biggest headache trigger in any glass is the alcohol itself. But some wines are clearly a safer bet than others. If wine tends to give you a headache, your best odds are with **lower-alcohol, lighter, younger wines**: a dry German Riesling Kabinett, Vinho Verde, Moscato d'Asti, Beaujolais, or a light Pinot Noir, drunk slowly, with food and water. The wines most often blamed for headaches are big, high-alcohol reds and cheap sweet wines, and people who drink those fast on an empty stomach.

What actually works for you depends on *why* wine hurts. For most people it's the amount of alcohol and how fast it goes down. For a smaller group it's histamine, tannins, or a migraine tendency. Sulfites, the ingredient everyone blames, are the cause far less often than the label warning suggests. This guide walks through each trigger, then gives you a practical shopping list for each one.

> **When to see a doctor.** A mild headache after a few glasses is common and usually harmless. But **get medical help right away (call 911 in the US)** if a headache is sudden and severe (the "worst headache of your life"), or comes with weakness, numbness, slurred speech, confusion, vision loss, a stiff neck, or fever. **Treat it as an allergic reaction and get help** if wine causes wheezing, trouble breathing, throat or lip swelling, or widespread hives, especially if you have asthma. **Book a regular appointment** if you get a headache from even a few sips most times you drink, your headaches are getting more frequent, you're over 50 and this is a new pattern, or you have migraines and wine keeps setting them off. A doctor can check for migraine, histamine problems, or medication interactions, which are all treatable.

## Why Wine Gives You a Headache: The Five Real Triggers

Before picking a bottle, it helps to know what you're avoiding. Headache researchers actually recognize two types of alcohol headache. One comes on quickly, within about three hours of drinking. The other is the delayed, next-morning hangover headache. Different wine ingredients seem to matter more for each.

### 1. Alcohol itself (the biggest factor for most people)

Alcohol widens blood vessels, pulls water out of your body through extra urination, disrupts sleep, and breaks down into a toxic by-product called acetaldehyde. All of those can cause a headache, and all of them scale with how much alcohol you drink. A 15% Zinfandel contains roughly 50% more alcohol per glass than a 10% Vinho Verde. Over a long dinner, that difference adds up to a whole extra drink or two without you noticing.

This is the trigger people most often overlook when they decide they're "sensitive to red wine." Many big reds are simply stronger than the whites people compare them to, and they're often poured in bigger glasses.

### 2. Histamine and other amines

Histamine is a compound your body uses in allergic reactions, and it's also produced during fermentation. Wine contains some, and red wine generally contains more than white, though the amount varies a lot from bottle to bottle. Most people break down dietary histamine easily with an enzyme called DAO. People with lower DAO activity can get headaches, flushing, a stuffy nose, or itchiness from histamine-rich foods and drinks. Alcohol may also slow the breakdown of histamine, which makes things worse.

We cover this in depth in our guide to [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol).

### 3. Tannins and other plant compounds

Tannins are the compounds that make red wine feel dry and grippy in your mouth. They come from grape skins, seeds, stems, and oak barrels. Some research suggests tannins and related polyphenols may affect serotonin, a brain chemical involved in migraine. The evidence isn't settled, but many migraine sufferers report that heavily tannic reds are worse for them than soft, light ones.

A newer idea comes from a 2023 lab study by researchers at the University of California, Davis, published in *Scientific Reports*. They found that a compound formed from **quercetin**, a natural plant flavonoid found in red wine, can block one of the enzymes that clears acetaldehyde. If that happens in people, acetaldehyde could build up and cause headaches, similar to the flushing some people get from alcohol. Quercetin levels tend to be higher in grapes grown with lots of sun exposure. This is still a lab finding and has not been confirmed in human drinkers, so treat it as a promising lead rather than an answer.

### 4. Congeners

Congeners are the by-products of fermentation and aging that give drinks their flavor and color. Darker drinks generally contain more of them, and red wine has more than white. Studies comparing dark and clear drinks have found that drinks higher in congeners tend to produce worse hangovers at the same alcohol dose. Our [congeners guide](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains which drinks carry the most.

### 5. Sulfites (less often than you'd think)

Sulfites are preservatives that keep wine from spoiling, and some are made naturally during fermentation. In the US, any wine with more than 10 parts per million must say "Contains Sulfites" on the label, which is why they get the blame.

Here's what that label leaves out. **Red wines usually contain fewer sulfites than white and sweet wines**, because tannins help protect red wine on their own. Yet red wine is the one people say gives them headaches. Many dried fruits contain far more sulfite than a glass of wine, and most people eat dried apricots without a headache.

True sulfite sensitivity does exist, but it's uncommon and usually shows up as breathing problems, mostly in people with asthma, rather than as a classic headache. For the full story, read our breakdown of [sulfites in wine and headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches).

## Best Wines If You Get Headaches: The Short List

These are the styles that combine lower alcohol, fewer tannins, and generally lower histamine. They're not guaranteed, but they're the best starting point for most people.

| Wine | Typical alcohol | Why it's a good pick | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| German Riesling Kabinett | About 8 to 10% | Low alcohol, no oak, no tannin, crisp | Some are off-dry; check "trocken" for dry |
| Vinho Verde (white) | About 9 to 11.5% | Light, young, low alcohol | Easy to drink fast |
| Moscato d'Asti | About 5 to 6% | Very low alcohol | Sweet, so it's easy to drink a lot |
| Sauvignon Blanc (cool climate) | About 11.5 to 13% | Unoaked, young, no tannin | Some New World versions run higher |
| Pinot Grigio (Italian) | About 12 to 12.5% | Light, simple, low in amines | Very cheap bottles vary in quality |
| Beaujolais (Gamay) | About 12 to 13% | One of the lightest, lowest-tannin reds | Cru Beaujolais can be fuller |
| Pinot Noir (cool climate) | About 12.5 to 13.5% | Thin skins, soft tannins | Warm-climate versions can hit 14%+ |
| Dry rosé | About 11.5 to 13% | Brief skin contact, so few tannins | Some are high in alcohol; check the label |

**Wines most often linked to headaches:** big, high-alcohol reds like Zinfandel, Amarone, Shiraz from warm regions, and ripe Cabernet Sauvignon (often 14.5 to 16%); heavily oaked wines; fortified wines like port and sherry (around 17 to 20%); and inexpensive sweet wines, which tend to be higher in sulfites and very easy to overdrink.

## The Best Wine for You Depends on Your Trigger

Most people never figure out which trigger is theirs, so they keep trying random "clean" bottles. A better approach is to match the wine to the likely cause.

### If you get headaches from any wine after two or three glasses

Your trigger is most likely the alcohol. Choose by the **ABV number on the label** before anything else. Aim for 12.5% or lower, and use the table above. Pour smaller glasses (a standard US drink of wine is 5 ounces, which is less than most restaurant pours), drink a glass of water with each glass of wine, and eat a real meal. This one change helps more people than any special wine. If you want to know how much you're actually drinking, see [how many drinks are in a bottle of wine](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-in-a-bottle-of-wine).

### If red wine gives you a headache but white doesn't

This is the classic pattern, and it points to histamine, tannins, or other red-wine compounds rather than sulfites. Try these, in order:

1. **Switch to light, young reds.** Beaujolais, cool-climate Pinot Noir, Frappato from Sicily, or a light Grenache. Avoid big, oaky, aged reds.
2. **Try a dry rosé or a crisp white** for a few weeks and see whether the headaches stop.
3. **Watch the alcohol** too, since full-bodied reds are usually stronger.

Our full guide to [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) covers this pattern in detail. If white wine is the one that gets you, our guide to [white wine headaches](/never-hungover/white-wine-headache) covers why that happens even without the tannins and histamine of red.

### If you get a headache within minutes of a single glass

A fast headache from a small amount is a different pattern from a hangover. It can point to histamine sensitivity, a migraine trigger, or a reaction to alcohol itself. Low-alcohol whites are your best option, but it's worth reading our guide to [headaches after just one drink](/never-hungover/headache-after-one-drink) and mentioning it to a doctor if it happens most times you drink.

### If you have migraines

Red wine is one of the most commonly reported migraine triggers, and large surveys of migraine patients regularly list it near the top of alcohol-related triggers. Interestingly, many of the same people say wine only sets off an attack some of the time, which suggests it often adds to other triggers like stress, poor sleep, or hormonal changes rather than acting alone.

If you have migraines, the best picks are low-alcohol, unoaked whites like Riesling Kabinett or Vinho Verde, and you'll probably do better keeping it to one glass on days you're already short on sleep or stressed. Our [migraine after drinking](/never-hungover/migraine-after-drinking) guide has more. If you take a migraine preventive or triptan, ask your doctor how alcohol fits in.

### If you also flush, itch, or get a stuffy nose

Headache plus flushing, a runny or stuffy nose, or itchy skin is a hint toward histamine. Lower-histamine choices are usually young, crisp whites and sparkling wines made without long aging. Some producers now test and market low-histamine wine, which can be worth trying, though label claims aren't standardized.

### If you're sure it's sulfites

If you have asthma and wine makes you wheeze, or you react badly to other high-sulfite foods like dried fruit, sulfites may genuinely be your issue. In that case:

- **USDA Organic wine** (in the US) cannot have sulfites added, so it typically contains only the small amount produced naturally.
- **"Made with organic grapes"** is a different label and may still have added sulfites.
- **Natural and low-intervention wines** often use little or no added sulfite, but they vary a lot, and some are higher in other compounds from wilder fermentation.
- **Dry red wine** is usually lower in sulfites than sweet white wine.

If sulfites cause breathing trouble, talk to a doctor, since that's a reaction that should be taken seriously.

## "Clean Wine," Organic, and Natural Wine: Do They Help?

"Clean wine" has become a big marketing category, often promising fewer headaches and no hangover. It's worth being clear about what that label means.

**"Clean wine" is not a regulated term.** There's no legal definition in the US, so any brand can use it. Some of these wines are genuinely made with fewer additives and lower alcohol, which can help. Others simply have no added sugar and a lot of branding. There is no good evidence that "clean wine" as a category prevents headaches or hangovers better than a regular wine with similar alcohol content.

**Organic wine** controls how the grapes are grown and, in the US, limits sulfite additions. That may matter if sulfites are truly your problem, but organic wine still contains the same alcohol, histamine, and tannins as any other wine.

**Natural wine** usually means minimal additives and minimal intervention. Many people enjoy it, and it's often lower in added sulfites. But a natural wine is not automatically lower in histamine, and an unfiltered, wild-fermented red can be high in compounds that some people react to.

**What actually helps:** ignore the marketing word on the front label and turn the bottle around. The ABV, the grape, the region, and whether it's oaked tell you far more than "clean."

## Best Wine for No Hangover: What Matters Most

People searching for a wine that won't give them a hangover are usually asking a slightly different question from those who get a headache while drinking. A hangover is mostly a dose problem. Every wine can cause one, and no wine is hangover-proof. The features that tend to give you a gentler morning are the same ones that help with headaches:

- **Lower alcohol.** This matters more than anything else. An evening of 9% Riesling is a different night for your body than an evening of 15% Shiraz, even if you drink the same number of glasses.
- **Fewer congeners.** Whites and rosés generally carry fewer than reds, especially aged and dark reds.
- **Drier styles.** There is no good evidence that sugar itself causes hangovers, but sweet wines are easier to drink quickly, can mask how strong they are, and often contain more sulfites.
- **Bubbles in moderation.** Sparkling wine may get alcohol into your bloodstream a bit faster, so the "light" feel of Champagne can be misleading. Sip it rather than knocking it back.

Our [wine hangover guide](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide) goes deeper into why wine hangovers can feel so rough.

## How to Read a Wine Label for Fewer Headaches

You don't need to be a wine expert to choose better. Here's what to look for on the bottle:

1. **ABV (alcohol by volume).** Look for 12.5% or lower. In the US, wine under 14% is allowed some leeway on the label, so a wine marked 13.5% might actually be a little higher or lower. Treat the number as a guide.
2. **Region.** Cool regions (Germany, northern France, Austria, northern Italy, Portugal's Vinho Verde area, New Zealand, Oregon) tend to make lighter, lower-alcohol wines. Hot regions often make riper, stronger wines.
3. **Grape.** Riesling, Gamay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Albariño, and Grüner Veltliner tend to be lighter. Zinfandel, Syrah or Shiraz, Petite Sirah, and Malbec tend to be heavier.
4. **Oak.** Words like "reserve," "barrel-aged," or flavor notes like vanilla and toast often mean oak, which adds tannin and other compounds.
5. **Sweetness.** "Trocken" on German wine means dry. "Brut" on sparkling wine means dry. Very sweet dessert wines are usually higher in sulfites.
6. **Vintage age.** Younger wines are generally simpler and lower in some aging-related compounds. If older reds give you trouble, stick to recent vintages.

## Habits That Matter More Than the Bottle

Even the "best" wine will give you a headache if you drink it the wrong way. These habits are simple, but they make a real difference:

- **Eat first and keep eating.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood, which softens the peak.
- **Alternate with water.** One glass of water for each glass of wine helps with the dehydration side of the headache.
- **Pace yourself.** Your liver clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies. Drinking faster than that lets alcohol and acetaldehyde build up.
- **Use smaller glasses.** Big glasses lead to bigger pours. A standard US drink of wine is 5 ounces.
- **Don't mix in a lot of other drinks.** Cocktails before dinner plus a bottle with dinner is a common recipe for a bad morning.
- **Protect your sleep.** Poor sleep is a headache trigger on its own, and alcohol already disrupts sleep. Stop drinking a few hours before bed if you can.
- **Keep a short log.** Write down the wine, ABV, how much you drank, and whether you got a headache. After four or five evenings, a pattern usually appears.

## What to Do If You Already Have a Wine Headache

If the headache shows up anyway, a few things can help:

- **Drink water or an electrolyte drink**, and eat something with salt and carbohydrates.
- **Rest in a dark, quiet room** if light and noise make it worse.
- **Caffeine** in a normal amount can help some headaches, especially if you usually drink coffee.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** Ibuprofen and aspirin can irritate a stomach already upset by alcohol, so take them with food and stick to the label. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is harder on the liver when combined with heavy drinking. Read our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) before reaching for it, and don't take painkillers "just in case" before bed.

For more ideas, see our [hangover headache relief guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025).

## Can Supplements Help With Wine Headaches?

Some people try supplements alongside the steps above. It's worth being realistic about what the evidence shows.

- **DAO enzyme supplements** are marketed for histamine intolerance. Some small studies suggest they may help people with low DAO activity, but the research is limited, and they won't help if histamine isn't your trigger.
- **Antihistamines** are sometimes used before wine by people who suspect histamine. Many cause drowsiness that alcohol makes worse, so check with a pharmacist before combining them. Our guide to [antihistamines and alcohol](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol) covers which ones raise the most concern.
- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for how it affects alcohol's effects. Animal research suggests it may support the breakdown of alcohol and acetaldehyde and affect how alcohol acts on the brain, but human data is still limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents wine headaches specifically, and it won't make high-alcohol drinking safe. Some people like taking it with water before or during a night of drinking as one part of a sensible routine. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts and what the research does and doesn't show.

No supplement replaces the two things that matter most: choosing a lower-alcohol wine and drinking less of it, more slowly.

## The Bottom Line

- No wine is guaranteed headache-free, because alcohol itself is the main trigger.
- Your best odds are with **lighter, lower-alcohol, unoaked wines**: German Riesling Kabinett, Vinho Verde, Moscato d'Asti, Sauvignon Blanc, Beaujolais, cool-climate Pinot Noir, and dry rosé.
- If red wine is the problem but white isn't, suspect histamine, tannins, or other red-wine compounds before sulfites.
- Sulfites are a real problem for a small number of people, mostly with asthma. Red wine is usually *lower* in sulfites than white.
- "Clean wine" is a marketing term, not a standard. Read the ABV, grape, and region instead.
- Eat, pace yourself, alternate with water, and keep track of what works.
- See a doctor for sudden severe headaches, neurological symptoms, breathing trouble, or headaches from very small amounts of wine.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What wine is least likely to give you a headache?**

Lighter, lower-alcohol, unoaked wines are your best bet. Good examples are German Riesling Kabinett, Vinho Verde, Moscato d'Asti, cool-climate Sauvignon Blanc, Beaujolais, light Pinot Noir, and dry rosé. No wine is guaranteed headache-free, because alcohol itself is the biggest trigger, so how much and how fast you drink matters as much as the bottle.

**Why does red wine give me a headache but white wine doesn't?**

Red wine usually contains more histamine, tannins, and other plant compounds than white wine, and many reds are also higher in alcohol. Any of those can trigger a headache. Sulfites are an unlikely culprit in this case, because red wine generally contains fewer sulfites than white wine. Try lighter, younger reds like Beaujolais or Pinot Noir, or switch to a crisp white or dry rosé.

**Is sulfite-free wine better for headaches?**

Only if sulfites are actually your problem, which is uncommon. True sulfite sensitivity mostly causes breathing symptoms, usually in people with asthma, rather than a typical headache. For most people, a sulfite-free or USDA Organic wine with the same alcohol content will cause the same headache as a regular one. If you do react to sulfites, USDA Organic wines in the US cannot have sulfites added.

**Does clean wine prevent headaches?**

There is no good evidence that "clean wine" as a category prevents headaches or hangovers. "Clean wine" is a marketing term with no legal definition in the US. Some of these wines are lower in alcohol or additives, which can help, but you'll learn more from the alcohol percentage, grape, and region on the label than from the word "clean."

**What is the best wine for no hangover?**

No wine is hangover-proof, since hangovers are mostly about how much alcohol you drink. The gentlest choices are lower-alcohol whites and rosés, which also tend to have fewer congeners than dark, aged reds. A dry Riesling Kabinett or Vinho Verde at 9 to 11% alcohol gives you far less alcohol per glass than a 15% red. Eat, drink water between glasses, and pace yourself.

**Does cheap wine cause more headaches than expensive wine?**

Price alone doesn't decide it. Some inexpensive wines are sweeter, higher in sulfites, and easy to drink quickly, which can lead to worse mornings. But many expensive wines are big, ripe, high-alcohol reds, which are among the most common headache triggers. A modest bottle of light, low-alcohol wine is often a better choice than a pricey 15% Cabernet.

**Can I take something before drinking wine to avoid a headache?**

Eating a proper meal and drinking water are the most reliable steps. Some people with suspected histamine sensitivity try DAO enzyme supplements or antihistamines, but evidence is limited and some antihistamines cause drowsiness that alcohol worsens, so check with a pharmacist first. Avoid taking painkillers before drinking "just in case," since they can add stress to your stomach or liver.

**When should I worry about a headache after drinking wine?**

Get emergency care if the headache is sudden and severe, or comes with weakness, numbness, slurred speech, confusion, vision changes, a stiff neck, or fever. Wheezing, swelling, or hives after wine may be an allergic reaction and also need prompt help. See a doctor if small amounts of wine regularly cause headaches, or if your headache pattern is new or getting worse.
